Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Does a Shorter Working Week Raise Productivity? A Synthesis of Five Sources

*Evidence briefing. Prepared for a working group on working-time policy.*

## Purpose

This briefing weighs five pieces of evidence on whether reducing the working week by a fifth, with pay maintained, raises productivity: the Halden multi-organisation pilot (source 1), the Varden County randomised trial at nine months (source 2), a re-analysis of the Halden pilot (source 3), a meta-analysis of 23 studies (source 4), and the 24-month follow-up of the Varden trial and of 14 Halden organisations (source 5). It adds no new data. Its aim is to state what the five together support, at the strength they support it, and what they leave open.

## 1. What each source contributes, and how later sources qualify it

**Source 1** established that many organisations that volunteered could cut scheduled hours by 20% with little change in reported output, and reported a 23.4% gain in output per hour, gains in every sector, large falls in sickness and resignations, and 92% continuation. Taken alone, it suggests a large, general effect.

**Source 2** was the first randomised evidence, with record-based output and actual hours. It introduced the distinction that the rest of the body depends on: between discretionary work, where output can be produced at any time within a deadline, and coverage-bound work, where output depends on presence while demand arrives. Per actual hour, output rose 12.5% in case-processing and 6.7% in counter work; per employee it was roughly unchanged in the first and fell 11.4% in the second. It also showed that actual hours fall less than scheduled hours, and that dividing by scheduled hours inflated the case-processing estimate from 12.5% to 22%.

**Source 3** found that source 1's figures were inflated in several documented ways: seven of nine withdrawals occurred after the schedule began, mostly for workload reasons, not "during the preparation phase"; manager-reported output exceeded record-based output by 3.8 points; actual hours fell 14.1%, not 20%; and the 1.4% revenue rise was a real fall of about 2.6% after inflation of 4.1%. Correcting what could be corrected reduced the per-hour gain to 10.8% in a subset. These findings stand. Source 3 then went further, concluding that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact, attributing the remainder to novelty on the basis of an extrapolated survey trend, and dismissing source 2's meetings hypothesis as post hoc. Those further claims do not survive later evidence.

**Source 4** placed both studies in a wider literature. Its pooled per-hour estimate of 13.4% is inflated by the same features source 3 identified; the estimates from controlled designs (+8.2%), actual-hours studies (+7.9%), record-based studies (+9.7%), controlled discretionary studies (+9.6%) and bias adjustment (+9.1%) converge on roughly 8 to 10%. Its work-type moderator generalises source 2: per-worker output fell about 9% in coverage-bound settings, consistently, and was roughly maintained in discretionary ones. It rejected source 1's sector-general claim and source 3's artifact claim. Its own claim that effects show no decay was wrong, for the reason source 5 gives.

**Source 5** applied the strictest standards in the body: randomisation, record-based output, log-measured hours and a two-year horizon. The per-hour gain in case-processing declined from 12.5% to 8.5% (log hours) but remained clearly above zero. Output per employee stood at −3.4%, with a confidence interval including zero. A registered mediation test attributed 47% of the gain to fewer recurring meetings and 18% to reduced fatigue. Source 4's "no decay" conclusion rested on four long-follow-up studies, all uncontrolled and using scheduled hours. The counter arm was ended at month 12.

## 2. Weighing the estimates

**Table 1. Estimates of the change in output per hour, ordered by strength of design**

| Estimate | Source | Change per hour |
|---|---|---|
| Uncontrolled, manager-reported, scheduled hours | 1 | +23.4% |
| Uncontrolled survivors, records, actual hours, 24 months | 5 | +11.8% |
| Uncontrolled subset, records, actual hours, 6 months | 3 | +10.8% |
| Meta-analysis, all studies | 4 | +13.4% |
| Meta-analysis, bias-adjusted | 4 | +9.1% |
| Meta-analysis, controlled discretionary | 4 | +9.6% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 9 months, timesheets | 2 | +12.5% |
| Randomised, case-processing, 24 months, system logs | 5 | +8.5% |
| Randomised, counter work, 9 months | 2 | +6.7% |

Estimates fall as designs strengthen and stabilise around 8 to 10% for discretionary work. The figure of more than 20% is not supported by any design that measures actual hours.

## 3. What the body supports

Read as a whole, the five sources support a conditional answer.

1. **Per hour, yes, by a moderate amount.** In discretionary work, a 20% cut in scheduled hours raises output per actual hour by roughly 8 to 10% under controlled measurement, with some decline from the first year to the second but no sign of disappearing within two years. The headline figure of more than 20% is an artifact of scheduled-hours denominators, manager-reported output and selection.
2. **Per worker, no.** Because actual hours fall by 11 to 14%, not 20%, a per-hour gain of 8 to 10% roughly offsets the hours cut but does not exceed it. Output per worker in discretionary work is around 2 to 4% lower than it would have been, with intervals that include zero. "Same output in four days" is close to true there; "more output" is not supported.
3. **In coverage-bound work, the answer is no on any measure that matters to the people served.** Output per worker falls by about 9 to 11%, waits lengthen, and maintaining service requires about 12% more staff. Per-hour gains exist but are small. This is the most consistent finding in the body.
4. **About half the per-hour gain in the best-measured setting comes from removing recurring meetings**, a smaller part from reduced fatigue, and about a third is unexplained.
5. **Sickness absence and resignations fall substantially** in every source that measured them (by roughly 27 to 36% for sick days). These are real benefits, but they are not themselves productivity, and the body does not estimate how far they offset per-worker output losses.

Whether "productivity" rises therefore depends on whether it is measured per hour or per worker, and on whether output in a given role depends on presence. Both slogans, "a four-day week makes people more productive" and "the gains are a mirage", are wrong as stated.

## 4. What the body leaves open

- **Is the hours cut necessary for the gain?** About half the per-hour gain runs through cutting meetings. Two control offices that audited meetings without cutting hours saw a 4.1% per-hour rise, but that is two offices without a comparison group. No study had an arm that reorganised work without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone would capture much of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and last, is not settled by this body.
- **Beyond two years.** No controlled evidence extends past 24 months. The per-hour gain declined between 9 and 24 months; whether it stabilises or continues to decline is unknown.
- **The unexplained third** of the per-hour gain has no tested mechanism.
- **Manufacturing and shift production** are almost absent from the evidence (two studies, both mixed).
- **Private-sector controlled evidence** is thin; the strongest designs are in public administration.

## 5. Bottom line

A 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay raises output per hour by roughly 8 to 10% in discretionary work, about half of it through fewer meetings, which roughly but not fully offsets the hours lost; in coverage-bound work it reduces output and service unless staff are added. Whether the gain requires the hours cut, or could be had by reorganising work alone, remains open.

</document>
response:
# Critical Reading: The Evidence Briefing

This is a good synthesis. It describes the five sources accurately, reaches the right overall conclusion, and makes the most important distinction clear: productivity per hour versus per worker, and discretionary versus coverage-bound work. Its conclusions are close to the ones I reached across the earlier readings.

Its weaknesses are of three kinds:

- it repeats a few of the sources' own overstatements without correcting them;
- it treats the sources as more independent than they are;
- it leaves out cost, which is what a policy working group needs most.

## 1. What it gets right

- **It accepts Source 3's documented corrections while rejecting its "entirely an artifact" conclusion.** This is the right split.
- **It says the 20%+ figure fails under any design that measures actual hours.** That is accurate and stated plainly.
- **It treats coverage-bound work as the most consistent finding.** All five sources support this.
- **It distinguishes sickness and turnover benefits from productivity**, and says the evidence doesn't show how far they offset lost output.
- **It frames the key open question correctly:** whether the gain requires the hours cut, or could be had by reorganising work alone.
- **It rejects both slogans** ("more productive" and "a mirage") as wrong as stated.

## 2. Overstatements carried over from the sources

**It compares different measures when describing decline.** Section 1 says the gain "declined from 12.5% to 8.5% (log hours)." This repeats Source 5's summary, which compares a timesheet figure at 9 months with a log-hours figure at 24 months. The like-for-like fall is 12.5% to 9.8%, about a fifth rather than a third. The confidence intervals also overlap heavily (+6.9 to +18.4 against +4.6 to +15.2).

**It calls the meta-analysis "wrong" about decay.** Source 5 showed the meta-analysis's no-decay claim was *unsupported*, because the four long-run studies were all uncontrolled. Source 5 did not show it was false. Its own decline is not statistically established.

**It omits the control-group contamination.** Two of seven Varden control offices ran meeting audits in month 15 and gained about 4% per hour. That narrows the treatment–control gap and makes part of the "decline" an artifact. A briefing that relies on this decline should mention it.

**It presents the mediation shares as settled.** The 47% / 18% / 35% split comes from:

- the same seven treated offices that generated the meetings hypothesis, so it is a pre-specified test, not an independent replication;
- 14 clusters;
- a model that assumes no unmeasured confounding and no interaction between meetings and fatigue.

There is also unresolved tension in the figures. On timesheet hours, treated staff's non-meeting time fell about 3% and output per worker fell 3.4%. That suggests output per non-meeting hour barely changed. If so, meetings may account for nearly all of the gain, not half. The briefing should say the split is uncertain in both directions.

## 3. It treats overlapping sources as independent

The five sources rest on about two underlying datasets plus a meta-analysis that includes both:

- **Halden data** appears in sources 1, 3, 4 and 5.
- **Varden data** appears in sources 2, 4 and 5.

So the nine estimates in Table 1 are not nine independent confirmations. "Converge on 8 to 10%" overstates the evidence. The meta-analysis subgroups also overlap with each other, as the meta-analysis itself notes.

**Table 1 is not actually ordered by design strength.** It is labelled that way, but:

- the meta-analysis figure for all studies (+13.4%) appears below two uncontrolled subsets;
- counter work (+6.7%) appears last, as if it were the strongest design, when it differs by type of work rather than by design.

"Estimates fall as designs strengthen" is also too neat. The strongest design at 9 months (+12.5%) is higher than the corrected uncontrolled subsets (+10.8%, +11.8%). The data show something different. **How hours and output are measured matters more than whether there is a control group.** Once records and actual hours are used, controlled and uncontrolled estimates fall in a similar range of about 8.5–12.5%.

## 4. Generalising from a single trial

Several statements rest on one public employer with 7 v 7 offices, but the briefing presents them as general:

- **"No sign of disappearing within two years."** This rests on one controlled study.
- **"About half of it through fewer meetings."** The bottom line applies this to all discretionary work, but it comes from one county's case-processing offices.
- **"Maintaining service requires about 12% more staff."** This was one county's estimate. Its accompanying +9% cost figure looks low: 12% more staff serving the same demand implies about +12% cost per contact.

The limitations section says controlled evidence is mostly from the public sector. The bottom line doesn't carry that qualification.

## 5. Smaller inaccuracies

**"Same output in four days" is misleading.** Actual hours fell 11–14%, not 20%. Staff worked overtime and on their days off. The accurate statement is "nearly the same output from about 4.4 days of actual work." That difference matters for anyone expecting a clean four-day week.

**The per-worker range may be too narrow.** If actual hours fall 11–14% and output per hour rises 8–10%, output per worker comes out between about −2% and −7%, not 2–4%. The observed estimates (−2.1% and −3.4% at Varden, and −2.7% in the meta-analysis's controlled discretionary studies) fit the narrower range. But the briefing's own arithmetic supports a wider one.

**The per-hour gain in coverage work is called real.** As noted in earlier readings, the +6.7% in coverage work is probably mostly a queueing effect. Fewer staff serving the same demand are idle less often, while the public waits longer. It is a cost passed to the public, not an efficiency gain.

**It suggests sickness reductions might offset lost output.** Output per FTE already reflects fewer sick days, because healthier staff are present more often. Only the turnover savings, such as recruitment and training, sit outside the output figures. Treating the sickness benefit as a separate offset would count it twice.

**It drops some nuance from the sources:**

- **A marketing agency in Source 5 reverted over client deadlines.** This shows coverage-like obligations inside work normally classed as discretionary.
- **Backlogs and deadline compliance have never been reported.** Source 2 raised this risk, and it is still unmeasured.
- **The original Halden paper misdescribed its attrition.** The briefing mentions it but understates its significance for trusting that source.

## 6. The main omission: cost

The briefing is written for a policy working group, but it never turns the findings into cost:

| Setting | Implication from the evidence |
|---|---|
| Discretionary work | Output per worker falls about 2–4% at full pay, so **labour cost per unit of output rises about 2–4%**, more if overtime is paid at a premium. |
| Coverage-bound work | Keeping service the same needs about 12% more staff, so **cost per unit rises about 10–12%**. |
| Offsets | Lower turnover reduces recruitment and training costs. These savings have not been quantified in any source. |

None of the five sources reports cost per unit of output. That is the most decision-relevant gap in the evidence, and it should appear prominently in Section 4. The briefing's answer, "same output, fewer hours," sounds like a cost-free gain. The evidence says it is a modest cost increase that buys real welfare and retention benefits. Whether that trade is worthwhile is a policy judgement, but the group should see it as a trade.

## 7. Suggested revision of the bottom line

> In discretionary work, a 20% cut in scheduled hours at full pay reduces actual hours by about 11–14% and raises output per actual hour by roughly 8–12%. Output per worker falls slightly (about 2–4%), so labour cost per unit of output rises modestly. In the one setting where mechanisms were tested, much of the gain, possibly most, came from removing recurring meetings. The gain persisted to 24 months in one randomised trial, possibly with some decline. In coverage-bound work, output and service fall unless staff are added, at an estimated 10–12% higher cost per unit. Sickness absence and resignations fall substantially in both. The central open question is whether reorganising work, especially cutting meetings, could deliver most of the per-hour gain without the hours cut. The obvious next study would test this with a trial arm that reorganises work without cutting hours.
